Indian Financial System: Markets, Institutions and Regulators

A financial system moves money from people who have savings to people and businesses who need funds. This guide maps its four parts: institutions, markets, instruments and regulators.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

What a financial system does

Households save more than they spend, while companies and governments usually need more money than they have. The financial system connects the two, and in doing so it also sets prices for money, spreads risk and makes payments possible.

  • Mobilises savings into investment.
  • Prices money and risk through interest rates and market prices.
  • Provides liquidity, so that investors can get out of their investments.
  • Runs payment systems such as UPI, NEFT and RTGS.

The four components

ComponentWhat it isExamples
InstitutionsOrganisations that collect and channel moneyBanks, NBFCs, insurers, mutual funds, pension funds
MarketsPlaces where financial claims are issued and tradedMoney market, capital market, forex market
InstrumentsThe contracts themselvesDeposits, shares, bonds, T-bills, derivatives
RegulatorsBodies that set and enforce rulesRBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA

Money market and capital market

The main dividing line among financial markets is the time period. Money market instruments run for up to one year; capital market instruments are longer.

BasisMoney marketCapital market
PeriodUp to 1 yearMore than 1 year
InstrumentsT-bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, repoShares, bonds, debentures
ParticipantsBanks, RBI, large institutionsCompanies, institutions, retail investors
Main regulatorRBISEBI
PurposeShort-term liquidityLong-term finance

Who regulates what

  • RBI: banks, NBFCs, monetary policy, payment systems and foreign exchange.
  • SEBI: stock exchanges, brokers, mutual funds, listed companies' disclosures and investor protection.
  • IRDAI: insurance companies and policies.
  • PFRDA: the National Pension System and pension funds.
  • Ministry of Finance: overall policy; the Ministry of Corporate Affairs administers company law.

Direct and indirect finance

In direct finance, savers buy securities issued by the user of funds, as in an IPO or a bond issue. In indirect finance, an intermediary stands between them: you deposit money in a bank, and the bank decides whom to lend it to. Intermediaries earn a spread, and in return they reduce risk through diversification and credit checks.

Exam and interview questions

What are the components of the Indian financial system?

Financial institutions, financial markets, financial instruments and regulators, with financial services connecting them.

What is the difference between the money market and the capital market?

The money market deals in funds for up to one year and is regulated mainly by the RBI. The capital market deals in longer-term funds through shares and bonds and is regulated mainly by SEBI.

Who regulates mutual funds in India?

SEBI regulates mutual funds. AMFI is the industry association, not a regulator.
